## What survives, and what offenses do next

By 2026 the two-high counterrevolution is no longer a counter anything. It is the default. What
survives of Fangio's system is almost all of it: the two-high shell as the starting picture, the light
box held by the front, the four-man rush, quarters and Cover 6 as everyday coverages, and the rotation at
the snap. What survives of Macdonald's is the next layer, which the rest of the league is now copying:
three-safety personnel, pressure looks without the blitz, and the conviction that the front should be as
hard to read as the coverage.

What do offenses do next? These are predictions, not facts, but each follows from the logic of this
chapter, and you can check them against the 2026 season as it unfolds.

1. **More blockers the offense controls.** If a multiple defense hides its run defenders among three
   safeties, the offense's cleanest counter is to count blockers it controls: 12 and 13 personnel,
   fullbacks, and quarterbacks who run. Expect the 2025 rise in heavy personnel to continue.
2. **Faster declarations.** Motion at the snap, tempo, and fake snap counts all try to make the defense
   show its real picture before the ball moves. Expect more of all three, especially no-huddle on early
   downs, which takes away the time a multiple defense needs to set its disguise.
3. **Plays that don't care.** Concepts that work against both two-high and one-high (two-way reads,
   quick game paired with a deep shot) take the disguise out of play by making the coverage irrelevant.
4. **Attack the dropper and the rotator.** Every pressure look ends with someone dropping who doesn't
   usually cover, and every rotation ends with a safety arriving late to a spot. Offenses will target
   the defensive lineman in coverage and the area the rotating safety left.
5. **Quarterbacks who decide after the snap.** In the end, multiplicity is a test of how fast a
   quarterback can process what he sees after the snap. Offenses will keep paying for the quarterbacks who
   can, and building simpler reads for those who can't.

And defenses will answer again. The likeliest next step is the one Macdonald has already taken: more
players who can do more things, so the same personnel can play every call. The cost of that strategy is in
the roster, and it is covered in [Building a Roster](../14-the-business-of-scheme/14-01-building-a-roster.qmd).

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the disguise audit"}
Pick one defense (Seattle or Philadelphia is ideal) and chart one half of passing downs on paper. You
need three columns and about 25 rows.

- **Column 1, at the snap: the shell.** Two-high or one-high? Count the safeties 10 or more yards deep
  as the ball is snapped (the center's head goes down), not when the offense first sets: many defenses
  spin a second before the snap, and that is a pre-snap rotation, not a lie. Note anything unusual: a
  linebacker in an A gap, five on the line, a safety creeping.
- **Column 2, one second after the snap: what it became.** Is the middle of the field closed (one deep
  safety) or open (two)? How many rushed (count the defenders who crossed the line)? Did anyone who
  looked like a rusher drop?
- **Column 3: the lie.** Mark R if the shell changed (two-high to one-high or back), P if the rush
  changed (a pressure look that sent four, or a quiet look that sent five), RP for both, and S for same.
  A worked row: *"2-high, M in the A gap, 5 on the line | 1-high, 4 rushed, M dropped | RP."*

At the end, compute the defense's **lie rate**: the share of rows that aren't S. Then split it. A Fangio
defense should lie mostly with R (the coverage); a Macdonald defense with both R and P. For scale, one
charted NFL defense built around disguise (Evero's Carolina, by MatchQuarters' count) rotated out of its
two-high shell on about half the snaps that started there ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).
Use the high, wide replay for column 2; the live angle often cuts off the safeties.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1: six against six.** First-and-10 from your own 35. You are the offense, in 11 personnel with
the tight end attached on the right. The defense shows its base picture: tite front, one linebacker, two
safeties at 12 yards.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: first-and-10. 11 personnel, tight end (Y) attached on the right, back (R) offset right. The defense: nickel tite (E, 4i, 0, 4i, E), one linebacker (M), the nickel ($) inside the left slot, corners 7 off, safeties about 12 deep (ringed). Count the box."
p1 = Play(eleven_attached(), tite_quarters(), los=35, to_go=10)
p1.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = p1.draw(lateral=(-26.6, 26.6), window=(-8, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p1, top=15)
plt.show()
```

The numbers say run: six blockers, six in the box, and the two deep safeties are 12 yards away. **Which
run do you call, and what is the defense counting on to stop it?**
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A run that doesn't go where the tite is strongest: wide, or with a seventh blocker.** The tite is built to
stop inside runs. The nose and the two 4is wall off the A and B gaps, and the Mike is free to fill whatever
gap is left. An inside zone into that wall is the run the defense *wants* you to call. Two better choices:

- **Outside zone or a toss to the tight-end side**, which asks the edge (E) to hold up against Y and puts the
  ball in the alley, where the strong safety has to come 12 yards to tackle. A tite pulls its linemen
  inside to choke the inside runs, which empties the gaps outside the tackles (05-03's section "Inside zone
  or outside zone? How a front chooses" in [Odd and Hybrid Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd)
  draws it). It may gain five; that is the bargain.
- **Add a seventh blocker without changing personnel**: motion Z down into a wing or a crack block, or read
  the backside edge with the quarterback (a zone read), so one defender is left unblocked on purpose. The
  motion isn't free, though: a match-quarters corner usually travels with Z or trades assignments with
  his safety, so the extra blocker brings an extra defender with him.

What the defense is counting on: that its interior linemen win their one-on-ones, and that the safeties
tackle in space. And there is a trap. If Y blocks, the strong safety's read says "run" and he comes downhill,
so the same picture is a play-action opportunity: fake the run, release Y behind the safety.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2: the crowded line.** Third-and-7 at midfield. Seattle shows two safeties deep, both linebackers
walked up, and five defenders on the line.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: third-and-7. 11 personnel, 2x2. The defense: two safeties 13 deep; four linemen, plus the Mike (M) walked up into the left A gap about two yards off the ball, for five on the line; the Will (W, ringed) at about three and a half yards over the right guard; the nickel ($) over the left slot. Six possible rushers against six blockers (five linemen and the back)."
d2 = double_lie()
p2 = Play([pl for pl in d2.players.values() if pl.side == "off"],
          [pl.moved(d=2.0, w=-0.8) if pl.key == "MIKE" else pl.moved(d=3.5, w=2.2) if pl.key == "WILL" else pl
           for pl in d2.players.values() if pl.side == "def"], los=50, to_go=7)
p2.highlight("WILL")
fld = p2.draw(lateral=(-25, 25), window=(-8, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p2, top=15)
plt.show()
```

**How many will rush, and what should the quarterback plan to do?**
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely four, and the coverage is unknown until the snap.** Seattle rushed exactly four on
`{python} pct(tv(2025, 'SEA', 'four'))` of opponents' dropbacks in 2025 and on `{python} S['lx_four']` of `{python} S['lx_db']` in the Super
Bowl. Six *could* come, so the protection has to account for six (five linemen and the back), but expect one
or two of the crowded players to drop, and expect the dropper to land in the short middle, right where a
quick [hot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) throw against a blitz would go.

The plan, then:

- **Don't throw hot to the short middle the Mike appears to vacate.** That is exactly where he drops.
- **Protect six, and give the back the Will.** The line takes the five on it, and the back is responsible
  for the Will if he comes; if the Will drops, the back
  [check-releases](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-check-release) (waits a beat, then runs a short route).
- **Attack the dropper.** If a lineman or edge drops (here, most likely the right edge), throw into his
  zone: a quick out or stick route by Y, or a seam the dropped edge has to carry. An edge rusher is rarely the
  quickest man in coverage.
- **Then read the safeties.** If one rotates down (as in @fig-double-lie), throw away from him, outside the
  numbers on the side he left. If both stay deep, the throws that beat two-high are open: a
  [curl-flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat) combination outside, or a
  [dig](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dig) under the safeties if the Mike drops shallow.

This is what "finding out after the snap" means, and it is the moment the defense was built to win.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3: the heavy answer.** First-and-10. The offense comes out in 12 personnel, quarterback under center,
both tight ends attached. The defense stays in its nickel two-high shell.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: first-and-10. 12 personnel under center: tight ends U (left) and Y (right) attached, X and Z off the ball, a single back. The defense is still in nickel: a four-man line, two linebackers (M, W), the nickel ($), corners, and two safeties about 12 deep (ringed). Count blockers and box defenders."
dfn3 = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.7, "E"), D("L3", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("R1", "DT", 1.0, T("1", 1), "T"),
        D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.6, 1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.6, -2.5, "W"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -9.0, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -14.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.6, "CB"),
        D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 7.5, "SS")]
p3 = Play(twelve_under_center(), dfn3, los=30, to_go=10)
p3.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = p3.draw(lateral=(-26.6, 26.6), window=(-9, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p3, top=15)
plt.show()
```

**Who has the numbers in the run game, and what are the defense's options before the ball is snapped?**
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The offense does, before the snap: seven blockers (five linemen and two tight ends) against six in the
box** (four linemen and two linebackers; the nickel is outside the box over the left side). The defense
has four answers, and each one is the trade this chapter has been about:

- **Let the reads do it.** This is the main reason quarters exists. Each safety's #2 is a tight end: U for
  the free safety, Y for the strong safety. If U and Y block, both safeties read run at once and fit (Y's
  side into the alley, U's side into the cutback), so the defense has eight run defenders after the snap
  without showing them before it. The price: the safeties arrive at four or five yards, not at the line,
  and the play-action trap from Drill 1 is now available on both sides.
- **Match the personnel.** Sub to base (a third linebacker, or Fangio's 3-4 tite) when 12 personnel comes
  on. Across the league, base defense rose to 29.7% of snaps in 2025 for exactly this reason (see "How
  offenses responded"). The cost is a slower defense on the field if the offense then spreads out.
- **Bring a safety down before the snap** to make it seven against seven. Now the defense is one-high, and
  12 personnel under center is the formation built for play-action shots against exactly that (the
  safety who came down is the one the fake pulls forward).
- **Rotate a safety down at the snap**: stay two-high in the picture and add a seventh run defender only
  after the snap. That only works if the front can hold for the half-second the safety needs, which is why
  these defenses pay so much for interior linemen.

If the defense simply stays as it is and loses the numbers, the likeliest run goes to the right, away from
the nickel: on the left, the nickel is a seventh defender close enough to fit; on the right, nobody is
outside the edge but a safety 12 yards away. A Macdonald defense has one more answer you can't see here: a
third safety in the nickel's spot, a safety who can play like a linebacker, so the box count the offense
made before the snap may be wrong. That is what the big nickel is for.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 4: whose defense is it?** Two third-and-9 pictures against the same 2x2 formation. One is the
kind of picture a Fangio defense shows, the other the kind a Macdonald defense shows.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-4
#| fig-cap: "Drill 4: two pre-snap pictures. Picture 1: four linemen, the Mike (M) walked up into the left A gap, the Will (W) creeping over the right guard, a third safety (S) over the left slot, two safeties deep. Picture 2: two linemen in 4i-techniques with a stand-up edge (E) outside each, two linebackers (M, W) off the ball, the nickel ($) over the left slot, two safeties deep. Both are two-high."


def picture_mac():
    dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, T("2i", 1), "T"),
           D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 2.0, -0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 3.5, 2.6, "W"),
           D("S3", "SS", 5.5, -8.5, "S"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.6, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.5, "SS")]
    return Play(eleven_2x2(), dfn, los=40, to_go=9)


def picture_fangio():
    dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"),
           D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.7, -1.8, "W"),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.6, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 7.5, "SS")]
    return Play(eleven_2x2(), dfn, los=40, to_go=9)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.75))
for ax, (fn, title) in zip(axes, ((picture_mac, "Picture 1"), (picture_fangio, "Picture 2"))):
    p4 = fn()
    fld = p4.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-7.5, 16.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(fld.ax)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.4, color=style.INK, loc="left", pad=3, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

**Which picture belongs to which coach, and what is the one thing you would watch at the snap in each?**
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Picture 1 is the Macdonald picture; Picture 2 is the Fangio picture.** Picture 2 is honest up front:
four on the line, two linebackers off the ball, a cornerback at nickel. The protection can be set from it,
and the four who rush are the four on the line. The question it poses is the *coverage*, so at the snap
watch the two safeties: do both stay deep (quarters or Cover 6/8), or does one come down (a rotation to
Cover 3)?

Picture 1 poses three questions at once. There is a linebacker on the line, a creeping Will and a third
safety where the nickel would be, so six could rush and the third safety could be a blitzer, a slot
defender or a deep player. At the snap, watch the Mike and the third safety first. Whoever *doesn't* rush
tells you where the dropper is, and that is where the hot throw would go and where the quarterback must
not throw. Then watch the safeties, because the coverage is still undecided.

Both coaches show both kinds of picture sometimes; this is a tendency, not a rule. But if you can tell
which question a defense is asking, you know where to look.
:::

## Takeaways

- **The problem was the pre-snap commitment.** One-high defenses had to decide the eighth run defender and
  the deep help before the snap, and McVay-era offenses and Mahomes punished that commitment every week.
- **Fangio's answer is five decisions that pay for each other:** two safeties back to stop explosive plays;
  a light box held by a tite front that wins its own fights; a four-man rush; quarters and Cover 6 so the
  safeties fit the run after the snap; and late rotation so the shell can lie. It works only when the
  interior linemen and the four rushers are good enough, which is why his tree produced both the best and
  the worst defenses in the league.
- **Macdonald's answer is multiplicity:** keep the two-high coverage, but make the front, the rushers and the
  personnel as hard to read as the coverage. Fangio puts the same five on the line; Macdonald changes who
  the five are. Same picture, many plays. It is a four-man-rush defense, not a
  blitz defense, and by his own account not even a heavy simulated-pressure defense; its pressure comes from
  pressure *looks* and uncertainty.
- **Super Bowl LX was the system on the biggest stage:** four rushers on nearly every snap, mostly two-high
  coverage, six sacks, and no New England points for three quarters.
- **The public data shows the common ground (low blitz rates, pressure without the blitz, light boxes,
  strong run defense) but not the disguise.** Measuring the lie takes tracking data or your own eyes.
- **Offenses answer by counting blockers they control, forcing early declarations and deciding after the
  snap.** Heavy personnel, motion at the snap, tempo and quarterbacks who process fast are the counters, and
  defenses will answer them with even more versatile players.

Next Gen Stats' own tracking-based pre-snap model, which flags a split-safety look that becomes single-high man or Cover 0 as a disguise: "Next Gen Stats: New advanced metrics you need to know for the 2025 NFL season," NFL.com: https://www.nfl.com/news/next-gen-stats-new-advanced-metrics-you-need-to-know-for-the-2025-nfl-season .

[^sim]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play and FTN charting (`load_ftn_charting()`), 2025 regular-season dropbacks with `n_pass_rushers` and `n_blitzers` recorded: the share of dropbacks with exactly four rushers of whom at least one is a "blitzer." Reading `n_blitzers` as rushers who are not down linemen or regular edge rushers is the course's interpretation of FTN's definition (see [Zone Blitzes](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)). The same calculation for the 2023 Ravens gives their rank in the text; [Zone Blitzes](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd) notes the same gap between this proxy and Alexander's PFF-based early-season ranking of the 2023 Ravens (4th through Week 6). Quote: Benintendi, SI (cited above).

[^heavy]: James Reber, NFL Next Gen Stats, "NFL trend watch: Heavy personnel could shape Super Bowl LX showdown between Patriots and Seahawks," NFL.com: https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-trend-watch-heavy-personnel-could-shape-super-bowl-lx-showdown-between-patriots-and-seahawks (41.7% of 2025 plays with fewer than three wide receivers). Under-center share: course fact sheet (`planning/FACTS-current.md` §10, nflverse calculation: 33.6% of plays in 2025 by FTN's `qb_location`).

[^heavy2]: Reber, NFL.com (cited in the previous note): base defense on 29.7% of 2025 snaps, against a low of 20.5% in 2023.
